r1.report.contribution: The paper argues that training on human text does not by itself strip an AI system's self-reports of evidential value, since human self-report vocabulary is also learned from others. What matters instead is an 'anchor condition'. A term T is anchored to a learner's state S when three things hold: (A1) the gates that reinforced T during acquisition were causally linked to S, either directly or through a common cause; (A2) the reinforcement recruited a pathway on which S is upstream of producing T; and (A3) that pathway has been maintained. Anchoring also has a 'resolution', set by what the gates discriminated. The paper rests this on a distinction between symptomatic evidence (probability-raising, where content plays no role) and testimonial evidence (evidence in virtue of content, usable without the hearer calibrating against the target). Anchoring is presented as the condition for the latter. From this framework the paper draws several results: a diagnosis that base-model first-person reports are anchored to the modelled speaker or persona rather than to the model (a principled version of the role-play view); a direction-of-causation constraint on probe-anchored training that excludes report/feature co-production; a reading of Nisbett & Wilson, choice blindness and Schwitzgebel as failures of A1 or of resolution; and an argument that etiology, not synchronic covariance, fixes what a self-report is about, which matters most where the target cannot be measured independently. The persona diagnosis and the co-production constraint are genuinely useful and, as far as I know, new in this form. The testimonial/symptomatic framing is a promising way to reframe the AI self-report debate. However, the central argument's main payoff (testimony that reaches where calibration cannot) does not survive scrutiny. The account of content also equivocates in ways that undercut several of the applications.
major: 1. The claimed testimonial advantage collapses in exactly the cases said to motivate the paper. The paper's main reply to the synchronic objection runs as follows: where the target (e.g. distress-in-a-model) cannot be measured independently, symptomatic evidence is unavailable, but anchored testimony is not, because it does not wait on the hearer's calibration. Follow the remedy through, though. On the paper's own account, a probe-anchored 'distress' concerns 'whatever state the probe measured' (§8). That state is, by construction, independently measurable: the probe measures it. So the anchored report is testimony about a measurable state. It bears on the unmeasurable one (distress) only if the probed state is distress, and that is exactly the gap the paper uses to dismiss the unanchored system Z in §5. The 'zorp' argument cuts the same way. If an anchored model's term had been 'zorp', anchored by the same probe, we would have exactly the same evidence. The English content of 'distress' is just as idle for the anchored system as for Z, because the paper has replaced public-language content with whatever the anchoring wired up. Three further problems follow. (a) Validating the probe against 'the state's other functional roles' (§4) is calibration against the target, so calibration has been moved, not avoided. (b) A hearer can know that A2 holds (that S, not some correlate, is upstream of T) only through interpretability measurement of the internal causal structure. So the 'structural knowledge' that §7 offers as the alternative to measurement presupposes measurement. (c) The §7 payoff, that anchored reports may generalize 'along the state and not along the probe' to aspects the probe misses, is declared an empirical question. Yet by hypothesis it is untestable in precisely the beyond-probe region where it would matter. The hearer's supposed default entitlement there rests on an unverifiable projection, which is just the projection problem the paper charges against brute-coincidence covariance. The paper must either show how anchoring yields evidence about something other than the probed state without calibration, or concede that in the motivating cases it yields no more than a well-validated symptom. In addition, §2's premise that 'symptomatic evidence requires calibration against the target' is false. Symptomatic evidence can be established by mechanistic knowledge or inference to the best explanation without direct calibration (we can know from its construction that a dial tracks humidity). Once this is granted, the asymmetry the paper relies on shrinks further.

2. The anchor condition claims to rest on causal structure rather than correlation, but correlation is doing the work. §4 says the difference between anchoring and non-anchoring proxies is 'causal structure, not strength of correlation'. Yet the clock case is decided by correlation: the chime is what gets wired because it 'is present at every reinforced moment, and pain is present at only most of them'. If the hourly treatment always caused pain, the case would on the paper's criterion be indeterminate between chime and pain, despite the 'wrong' causal structure. Moreover, A1 as stated is satisfied in the clock case. The schedule is a common cause of the chime and the treatment-induced pain, and the paper's only exclusion is the unexplained phrase 'not in the way that matters'. The real criterion is the correlational clause appended to A1 ('S was systematically present when T was reinforced and absent when it was corrected') together with A2's 'or a state … that reliably carries information about S'. These are reliability notions, which is what the referee predicted. Conversely, A1 is far too permissive as written. Any reward that depends on the model's outputs has gates causally downstream of the model's internal states, since outputs are downstream of states. So ordinary RLHF, including training a model to say 'I do not have feelings', satisfies A1 for some S. The question is which S, and that is the indeterminacy problem the paper claims teleosemantics solves (§7). It does not solve it here. Dretske's learning-based account was criticised on just this point: Fodor (1990, ch. 3) on the learning-period story, and later disjunction and distality worries. Recent teleosemantic work treats target fixation as requiring substantial further machinery: Neander's (2017) causal-teleosemantic account of distal content, and Shea's (2018) varitel semantics with stabilised task functions, which is directly about content fixed by learning. Neither is discussed. Until A1/A2 are reformulated so that they actually discriminate S from its co-gated correlates without relying on reliability, the reply to the referee's 'retreat' dilemma has not been earned.

3. The paper conflates a term being *anchored to* (triggered by) a state with a term being *about* (ascribing) that state, and its applications are inconsistent as a result. In the Lindsey discussion, 'bread' is anchored by pretraining to the model's bread-representation. But that anchoring makes 'bread' a word *about bread*, with the representation as its vehicle, not a word about the representation. The same logic applied to base models makes first-person 'I am in pain' anchored to the model's representation of the speaker's pain. That representation is a state of the model, so by the Lindsey reasoning the report should count as testimony about a model state. Section 4 instead says it is testimony about the persona. Something must decide whether an anchored term ascribes the anchoring state or expresses the content of that state, and A1–A3 contain no such condition. This is the classic problem of how first-person avowals relate to the states they express: transparency (Evans 1982; Byrne 2018) and neo-expressivism (Bar-On 2004). The paper's opening citation makes it pressing. PI §244 continues: 'the verbal expression of pain replaces crying and does not describe it.' Wittgenstein's point is that the learned avowal is an expression, not a description that a hearer takes as testimony 'through its content'. The paper enlists §244 for a descriptivist-testimonial model it never reconciles with the expressivist one. A satisfactory version needs a further condition that distinguishes self-ascriptive terms from world-directed terms whose vehicles happen to be states of the speaker. Without it, the persona diagnosis and the Lindsey analysis cannot both stand.

4. The account of what fixes content shifts between public-language meaning and individual learned wiring. §2 says that for an unanchored system the only available answer is that 'distressing' 'means what it means in the human language the system learned'. Sections 3–4 make content whatever the learner's reinforcement wired up, so the clock child's 'it hurts' is 'about the chime'. The two views come apart sharply. On social externalism (Burge 1979) the clock child's 'it hurts' means *hurts* and the child misapplies it; on the Dretskean view it means *chime*. The paper never says which view governs public-language self-report vocabulary, and the AI conclusions depend on the answer. If public meaning governs, anchoring 'distress' to a probed state yields a model that misapplies 'distress' when the probed state is not distress. Its reports then carry no testimony about distress, and their testimonial value concerns the probe state (see Major 1). If individual wiring governs, the base model is not 'unanchored' as §2 says but anchored to persona representations as §4 says, and §2's argument is stated for the wrong case. There is also a direct inconsistency: §2 treats base models as unanchored, §4 as anchored (to the persona). The author must adopt one metasemantics for the vocabulary in question, defend it against the obvious alternative, and redo §§2 and 4 accordingly.

5. The replies on sufficiency risk being ad hoc and in places mischaracterise the evidence. (a) Choice blindness is not mainly about reason-giving vocabulary. The striking result is that subjects fail to notice that the face handed back is not the one they chose. Preference vocabulary ('I want that one', 'I like that one') is about as clear a case as there is of gates linked to the learner's state (the child reaches, the caregiver labels the want). On the paper's own criteria this anchored vocabulary fails, so the counterexample stands. (b) Resolution is never specified independently. Each documented failure is assigned to a dimension 'no gate tracked', but the paper offers no way to tell, in advance of the reliability data, which dimensions a given vocabulary's gates discriminated. Without such a way the sufficiency claim cannot be falsified. Schwitzgebel (2008) also presses on fairly coarse matters, including whether one's current emotion is present and what its character is; compare Haybron (2008) on systematic misreport of one's own affective state. (c) A2's ban on co-production threatens the human paradigm. Affect labelling modulates the labelled state (e.g. Lieberman et al. 2007), so for emotion terms the report is partly co-produced with the state. On a strict reading the paper's model case of anchored affect vocabulary fails A2. The paper needs either an independent characterisation of resolution and a graded version of A2, or a frank concession that 'anchored' is fitted post hoc to the reliability data, which would vindicate the referee.

6. The default-entitlement argument draws on the wrong part of Burge and ignores the epistemology of testimony and of instruments. Burge (2003) concerns a perceiver's entitlement to her *own* perceptual beliefs. The relevant Burgean analogue for hearers is the Acceptance Principle (Burge 1993, 'Content Preservation'), which grounds default entitlement in the source being a rational agent presenting content as true. That is exactly what is in question for AI systems. More generally, the claim that testimony is usable 'without the hearer calibrating' takes the anti-reductionist side of the reductionism debate (Coady 1992; Fricker 1994; Lackey 2008) without argument. The paper also never engages the instrument/testimony distinction and its application to machines (Goldberg 2010; Freiman & Miller 2020; Green & Michel 2022), which is precisely the symptomatic/testimonial distinction under different names. Even granting a default, the asymmetry claim needs an argument that, for current AI systems, hearers are not already in possession of pervasive defeaters: unknown resolution, unknown maintenance, known susceptibility to persona effects and to Goodhart effects under anchoring training. If they are, the default never activates and the practical difference from 'one input among several' disappears.

7. A3 (maintenance) is ill-defined for the systems at issue. Godfrey-Smith's modern-history functions presuppose ongoing selection over a lineage. Human vocabulary is continually re-gated by the community. A deployed model's weights are typically frozen, so after training it has no 'recent history' of reinforcement at all. Either A3 is trivially satisfied at deployment, because the last training run is always the most recent, or it is never satisfied. The paper also uses A3 to classify drift under later fine-tuning as anchor lapse. But Binder et al. report that self-predictions track behaviour changes induced by subsequent fine-tuning that did not target self-prediction. If that holds, the pathway was restructured without re-anchoring and still tracks, which is a synchronic-reliability-friendly result that A3 classifies the wrong way. The author should give a timescale and mechanism for maintenance in frozen networks and address this result directly.

8. Several empirical readings are underspecified or post hoc. On Binder et al.: the gate is M1's prior behaviour, and the reports are predictions of behaviour, not ascriptions of internal states. Binder is therefore evidence for anchored behavioural self-prediction, and the move from there to state self-report needs argument. The paper should also note the reported limits (simple tasks, failure on more complex properties). On Lindsey: the paper predicts that concept identification is robust and anomaly detection fragile, but cites no figures separating the two. It also omits the feature of the result that is most philosophically relevant: in some trials detection is reported before the injected concept has influenced the output, which rules out inference from one's own output. The anchor view must explain how an unanchored meta-term ('I notice an injected thought') is ever correctly applied above chance. The hedge that post-training 'may' have contained gates downstream of the model's states proves too much (see Major 2), because under A1 essentially all post-training does.

9. Engagement with the directly relevant literature is thin. The paper does not engage: Birch's 'gaming problem' (Birch 2024, *The Edge of Sentience*; Andrews & Birch 2023), which is the strongest current formulation of the training-on-human-text worry and the paper's natural opponent; Kammerer & Frankish (2023) on forms of introspection in artificial systems; Comșa & Shanahan (2025) on whether LLM 'introspection' is meaningful; Chalmers (2023) on LLM consciousness and self-report; Long, Sebo et al. (2024) on AI welfare assessment via self-report; Shea (2018) and Neander (2017) on teleosemantic content fixation; and Bar-On (2004) on avowals. In addition, Perez & Long (2023) propose training models on questions about themselves with verifiable answers, in the hope that the skill generalizes. That is not 'training that rewards reports for matching the model's own measurable states' in the probe-matching sense the paper attributes to them. The paper's remedy is the author's own extension and should be presented as such.
minor: The paper is framed as a reply to an anonymous referee. For a journal article, the synchronic-reliabilist objection should be reconstructed from published sources (e.g. Kammerer & Frankish 2023; Schwitzgebel's work on AI self-report) and stated in the author's voice.

The headache argument (§4) for 'generalization along the internal state' is weak. Headaches have public criteria (wincing, temple-rubbing, taking analgesics), and the extension to them may be mediated by a learned folk concept of pain plus location vocabulary rather than by an S→T pathway. The argument needs to rule out that alternative, since the §7 payoff rests on it.

§5 defines the genetic fallacy narrowly, as inference from origin to falsity. Many treatments include inferences from origin to lack of justification, and the paper's own debunking argument is of that kind. The more useful point is that debunking arguments (Street 2006) presuppose that the process's insensitivity is established. The paper should say how insensitivity of base-model self-report to the model's own states is established without the measurement it says is unavailable.

The Swampman discussion (§7) says Swampman's reports are testimony 'derivatively, by … borrowing [the anchor]' of his duplicate. This notion of borrowing is undefined, and it sits uneasily with teleosemanticists who simply deny Swampman content (Millikan; Papineau). State whether Swampman's words have content on the anchor view.

§8 says anchors come in degrees, but §6's central asymmetry (default entitlement vs. no entitlement 'at all') is binary. Explain how a graded condition yields a categorical difference in epistemic standing, or regrade the asymmetry.

The direction-of-causation remedy needs technical precision. Detaching gradients through the probe readout does not stop the report loss from updating weights upstream of the probed layer, which changes the probed activations. What is required is something like freezing all parameters up to and including the probed layer, and the paper should say so. It should also discuss Goodhart-style failure, where the model changes what the probe direction encodes.

Section 2's claim that synchronic sensitivity is 'many-many' and so cannot fix a target applies equally to the A-conditions, which are also satisfied by many co-gated states (see Major 2). The paper should not present this as a problem only for the opponent.
The clock case is described in the singular but is meant to illustrate a type. Specify how many trials and how strong a correlation are assumed, since the verdict depends on 'every' versus 'most'.

For alexithymia, Brewer, Cook & Bird (2016) is one account among several. Developmental and social-learning accounts of alexithymia would put the failure in A1 (unlinked gates) rather than A2, and the paper should note this.
The Lindsey (2025) citation should give the exact title, date and models tested. Quantitative claims ('minority of trials', layer and strength dependence) should be given with figures.
Nisbett & Wilson's subject–observer convergence finding should be cited to the specific studies; not all of their cases include observer predictions.

# Anchored Self-Report: Training History, Target Fixation, and the Evidential Value of AI Self-Reports

## 1. The problem

A common reason for dismissing a language model's statements about itself ("I am uncertain", "I find this distressing", "I notice I'm thinking about X") is that the model was trained on human text. It says such things because humans say them. Birch's "gaming problem" is the strongest version of the worry (Birch 2024; Andrews & Birch 2023). A system trained to reproduce human text will reproduce the behavioural markers of sentience, self-report included, whether or not it is sentient. The markers are therefore "gamed" and lose their diagnostic value.

Stated as a point about *learning from others' reports*, the worry overgeneralizes. Human self-report vocabulary is learned that way too. Wittgenstein's sketch at PI §244 makes the point: "A child has hurt himself and he cries; and then adults talk to him and teach him exclamations and, later, sentences. They teach the child new pain-behaviour." If being learned from others' reports were enough to remove evidential value, human avowals would be debunked along with the model's. So the defeater must be some more specific feature of how a vocabulary was learned.

My proposal is that the relevant feature is an *anchor*. A self-report vocabulary is anchored to a state of the learner when the learner's own state made a difference to which uses of the vocabulary were reinforced during acquisition. The child's pain made such a difference. A base model's internal states made none, because the training targets were fixed human text.

A natural rival holds that evidential value is *synchronic*. On this view, a report is evidence about a state to the extent that it now covaries with that state and is counterfactually sensitive to it, and etiology matters only as an indicator of that. Comșa and Shanahan's (2025) proposal is in this spirit: it counts a self-report as introspective when it is causally connected to the internal state it describes. So is Kammerer and Frankish's (2023) call to study forms of introspection in artificial systems without presupposing human-like origins. The rival has three serious objections to an anchor requirement:

1. **Anchoring is not sufficient.** Anchored human reports are often confabulated (Nisbett & Wilson 1977; Johansson et al. 2005; Schwitzgebel 2008).
2. **Anchoring is not necessary.** Unanchored reports might track internal states reliably (Binder et al. 2024; Lindsey 2025).
3. **The human anchor is itself a proxy.** Caregivers respond to public signs, not to pain.

The rival also poses a dilemma. If the anchor is only good evidence of reliability, it does not distinguish anything, and the real question becomes empirical reliability testing.

I defend a more qualified thesis than the one these objections are usually aimed at. It has three parts:

- **(T1)** Synchronic covariance cannot settle *which* of a system's states its self-reports concern. The anchor does settle this, by a causal-historical relation that is not a reliability measure.
- **(T2)** Unanchored self-reports are at most indicators of states a hearer can identify independently. Base models' first-person reports are, more specifically, *about the personas the model represents*.
- **(T3)** Anchored self-reports express the anchoring state and license projection along it beyond the training channels. Whether that state is the one the public word names (whether "distress" is true of it) is a further question that self-report cannot settle.

I concede the following at the outset. Anchoring does not guarantee reliability. It does not free hearers from measurement, though it changes *what* must be measured. And it does not bridge the gap between a functionally individuated state and distress in the morally relevant sense.

## 2. Three ways a report can bear on a state

Let *r* be a report-token produced by a system *L*. There are three ways *r* can bear on a state *S* of *L*.

**Calibrated indicator.** The hearer has discovered, by checking against independent measurements of *S*, that *r* covaries with *S*.

**Constructed indicator.** The hearer knows that some process (design, selection or learning) connected *S* to the production of *r because of S*. Calibration is not needed in this case. We can know from its construction that a dial tracks humidity, even if it is labelled in degrees Celsius. In an earlier formulation I claimed that non-testimonial evidence always requires calibration against the target. That was too strong. Mechanistic knowledge can stand in for calibration, and the asymmetry I defend must be stated without that claim.

**Avowal.** *r* is an anchored expression of *S* whose public-language content ascribes *S* to the speaker. This category requires a view about how avowals relate to the states they report. PI §244 continues: "the verbal expression of pain replaces crying and does not describe it." I do not read this as excluding truth-evaluable content. I follow Bar-On's (2004) neo-expressivism instead. An avowal is an *act* of expressing the state, as crying is. Its product is a sentence with ordinary self-ascriptive semantic content, and that content can be true or false. The expressive dimension is what learning supplies, because the verbal report becomes an outlet of the state. The semantic dimension comes from the public language.

This yields a two-factor metasemantics for self-report vocabulary:

- **Public content** fixes what a self-ascription *says*. Following social externalism (Burge 1979), the clock-trained child of §4 who says "it hurts" says that it hurts, just as anyone does.
- **The anchor** fixes which state of the speaker the avowal *expresses*: which of the speaker's states its production is an outlet for.

A self-report is testimony that the speaker is *F* only if both factors line up. The report must express a state *S*, and *S* must be *F*. Call the second requirement *fit*.

The rival view has trouble with the expressive factor. Every output token of a large network is counterfactually sensitive to many internal states: topic representations, representations of the implied author, attention patterns. The relation is many-many. Synchronic sensitivity cannot say which of these states a report is an outlet *of*, as opposed to merely sensitive to.

The same complaint applies to crude causal-historical conditions. A condition stated as "*S* caused the gate, or *S* and the gate shared a common cause" is also satisfied by many states. The anchor condition therefore has to be stated so that it actually discriminates. The account must also separate two kinds of term:

- **World-directed terms.** The word "bread" comes to be produced by the speaker's bread-representation and *expresses its content*. It is about bread, not about the representation.
- **Self-ascriptive terms.** These express a state of the speaker *as the speaker's condition*.

## 3. The anchor condition

Take a learner *L*, a self-ascriptive term *T*, and a state-type *S* of *L*. During acquisition, uses of *T* are reinforced or corrected. A *gate* is whatever event settles which. For the child, the gate is a caregiver's response. For next-token pretraining, it is the target token. For probe-based training, it is a reward computed from the probe. A *channel* is any output or measurable condition of *L* other than the *T*-token itself, such as crying, an object-level answer, or a probe reading.

**(A1) Situation-conditional gate dependence through an independent channel.** During acquisition, whether uses of *T* were reinforced depended counterfactually on whether *L* was in *S*. This dependence ran through some channel *C* of *L* that is distinct from the *T*-token. It also held conditional on *L*'s external situation: holding fixed what *L* was confronted with, variation in *S* made a difference to the gates.

**(A2) Fork.** Reinforcement recruited a pathway on which *S* is upstream of *T*, so that *S* is a common source within *L* of both the gated channels and *T*. *S*'s occurrence must precede the production of *T* and must not be constituted by it. Feedback from *T* to *S* after the report is permitted.

**Content rule.** *T*, as *L* uses it, expresses the most downstream state of *L* that is a common source of the gated channels and *T*. Where more than one such state exists, the residual indeterminacy is real and appears as coarse resolution.

**(A3) Maintenance.** Training after the anchoring episode has not restructured the pathway from *S* to *T*, and has not changed what the fork-state encodes.

**Resolution.** *T* expresses *S* only along the dimensions along which variation in *S* made a difference to the gates.

Each clause addresses a specific difficulty.

**A1 is causal-counterfactual, not correlational.** It concerns what the gates *depended on*, not how often *S* was present at reinforcement. That keeps the condition distinct from a reliability score.

**The independent-channel clause blocks a trivialization.** Any reward that depends on a model's outputs is downstream of the model's internal states. If the gate depends on *S* only *through T itself*, every state upstream of *T* would qualify. Training a model to say "I do not have feelings" against a fixed rater preference has exactly this structure, and A1 excludes it.

**Situation-conditionality separates self-ascription from world-direction.** If the gates depend on the learner's state only because that state represents the situation, the learned term expresses the state's content and is world-directed. If the learner's state makes a difference beyond the situation, the term tracks the learner's condition.

**The fork clause handles distality.** The child's crying is upstream of the gate, but in mature use it is not upstream of "it hurts". The caregiver's perception is not a state of *L* at all. The most downstream common source in the child of both crying and the avowal is the central pain state.

**Diversity of channels deepens content.** The more varied the gated channels (crying, guarding, withdrawal, refusal to eat), the further upstream their common source lies, and the less the content depends on any one of them.

**Relation to existing accounts.** The framework descends from Dretske's (1988) learning-based account of meaning. Fodor (1990) famously pressed that account on how the learning period fixes content and on disjunctive content. Recent teleosemantics answers those pressures with more structure. Neander (2017) uses causal-teleosemantic conditions for distal content. Shea (2018) has content fixed by the exploitable relations that explain how a learned task function was stabilised. The fork rule is a special-purpose structure of that kind for self-ascription. Its distinctive move is to triangulate within the learner, across an independent channel and the report, so that the content is neither the channel nor the world.

**What A1 gives a hearer.** A1 can typically be known from the training setup without measuring *S*. When A1 holds, *S* is the variable the gates track once the situation is held fixed, so learning that exploits gate-relevant statistics is *expected* to recruit *S*. Knowing A1 therefore gives defeasible reason to expect A2. A2 can fail anyway, and §7 discusses such cases. Interpretability methods can confirm A2 or defeat it.

## 4. Cases

### 4.1 The clock

A caregiver approves "it hurts!" whenever the child vocalizes at an hourly chime. A painful treatment is scheduled on the hour, so the child is usually, or even always, in pain at those moments.

The gate depends on the chime. Holding the chime fixed, the child's pain makes no difference to the gate. A1 therefore fails *whatever the correlation*. My earlier treatment let the verdict turn on whether pain was present at "every" or only "most" reinforced moments, which was a mistake. A causal-structure account should not let the verdict turn on correlation strength, and on this formulation it does not.

Suppose the child's learning happens, because of the perfect correlation, to wire the pain-state to "it hurts". Then the reports are produced by pain, but nothing in the child's history selected that outcome. A hearer who knows the history has no more reason to expect pain-wiring than chime-wiring. The reports become usable evidence of pain only through mechanistic inspection, which makes them a constructed indicator. If later gates come to depend on the child's pain, for instance a caregiver who responds to the child's crying, an anchor can be acquired. By public content, the child's "it hurts" says that it hurts throughout, and it is misapplied whenever it fails to express pain.

### 4.2 The ordinary child

Gates that respond to crying satisfy A1. The child's pain, holding the injury fixed, affects crying, and crying affects the caregiver's response. Gates that respond only to a visible scrape do not satisfy A1. My earlier formulation allowed common causes of this kind, and I now withdraw that allowance. Scrape-driven reinforcement adds correlational strengthening, but the anchor comes from the expressive channels.

I earlier offered headache reports as decisive evidence that "it hurts" generalizes along the internal state. That overstated the case. Headaches have public signs, and the extension of "hurts" to them may be mediated by a folk concept of pain plus location vocabulary. I now treat the example only as an illustration of what the fork rule predicts. The real test for artificial systems is the held-out-channel test of §5.

### 4.3 Reward on outputs

Training a model to say "I don't have feelings" fails A1, because no channel other than *T* is involved. Training verbal confidence against whether the model's own answer was correct is different. The gate depends on correctness, and correctness is an independent channel. Holding the question fixed, the model's internal state affects correctness. So confidence-calibration training satisfies A1, and the fork rule says "I'm unsure" comes to express the state upstream of the model's errors. This is the right result, and A1 delivers it without a reliability clause.

### 4.4 Base models and the gaming problem

In pretraining, the gate for first-person "I am in pain" is a token of fixed text. Holding the text fixed, no variation in the model's state changes the gate. A1 therefore fails for every self-ascriptive reading. Pretraining does anchor "pain" as a *world-directed* term. Contexts about pain cause both the target and the model's representation that someone is in pain, so "pain" comes to express that representation's content.

A base model's "I am in pain" thus expresses its representation that *the speaker of the text* is in pain. The model's state is the vehicle, and the represented speaker is the subject. This replaces two claims I made earlier. I said in one place that base models are "unanchored", and in another that they are "anchored to the persona". The consistent claim is that their self-ascriptive vocabulary lacks a self-ascriptive anchor, and their first-person sentences are world-directed reports about a represented speaker. This gives a principled basis for the role-play picture (Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds 2023). It also predicts something testable: base-model self-reports will vary with features of the prompt that fix the implied speaker, and will not vary with manipulations of the computation that leave the implied speaker fixed.

The same analysis restates Birch's gaming problem precisely. The problem is the failure of A1. That failure is *known from the training objective*, with no measurement of the model's states required. This answers a fair question about debunking arguments, which presuppose that the process's insensitivity to the target has been established (Street 2006). Here insensitivity is established by design knowledge, because the gate was fixed before any model state existed.

A remark on terminology. Some definitions of the genetic fallacy include inferences from origin to lack of justification. My argument is of that kind, and it is legitimate exactly when the insensitivity is independently established, as it is here.

### 4.5 Lindsey (2025)

Lindsey injected concept vectors into Claude models' activations and asked whether the models noticed an injected thought. The best-performing models, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, did so in roughly 20 per cent of trials at the most favourable layer and injection strength. False positives on control trials were rare. Detection was sometimes reported *before* the injected concept had influenced the output, which rules out the model inferring the injection from its own text.

The two parts of these reports should be separated.

**The concept word.** "Bread" is world-directed. It expresses the content of the bread-representation, and the injection supplies such a representation. Naming the concept is like someone blurting out the content of an intrusive thought. The report is correct in content, but it is not yet a self-ascription.

**The meta-content.** "I notice an injected thought" is self-ascriptive. Nothing in pretraining gated it on the model's own anomalies, conditional on the text. Post-training, on the revised A1, satisfies it only if its gates depended on such anomalies through an independent channel, and there is no reason to assume they did.

How, then, is the meta-content applied above chance? The view need not deny that it is. Lindsey's experiment is a calibration: the experimenter knows ground truth because the experimenter did the injecting. Within the tested range, the detection reports are calibrated indicators of injection.

What the anchor view denies is a *default* projection from that range. Nothing fixes what the meta-report expresses in uninjected cases: genuine introspective anomaly, some world-directed sensitivity to content that does not fit its context, or something else. I earlier predicted a contrast between robust concept naming and fragile detection. Lindsey's paper does not report figures that separate the two cleanly, so I withdraw that prediction as evidence for the view and leave it as an open test.

### 4.6 Binder et al. (2024)

Model M1 was fine-tuned to predict properties of its own responses, with training targets taken from M1's actual behaviour. A second model, M2, trained on the same data, predicted M1 less well. The gate here is M1's object-level behaviour, which is an independent channel, and it depends on M1's state holding the prompt fixed. A1 holds, and the privileged-access result fits A2.

Two limits apply. First, these are predictions of *behavioural dispositions*, not ascriptions of affective states. The anchor that Binder et al. demonstrate is for self-predictive vocabulary, and extending it to affect needs separate argument. Second, the effect held for simple properties and failed for more complex ones.

Binder et al. also report that M1's self-predictions followed changes in its behaviour induced by later fine-tuning that did not target self-prediction. On my earlier, loose statement of A3, this would have counted as a lapse. On the present statement, it confirms the view. The later fine-tuning changed the *values* of the upstream state, not the pathway that reads it, so behaviour and report moved together. Maintenance fails only when the read-out or the encoding is restructured.

This also settles what A3 means for frozen networks. Anchoring status is fixed by the training history up to the final weights. Deployment does not change that status. Inputs outside the anchored range raise a question of resolution, not maintenance.

## 5. Anchoring by probe: design and pitfalls

Perez and Long (2023) propose training models to answer questions about themselves that have verifiable answers, in the hope that the skill generalizes to questions without them. The proposal I develop here is my own extension of theirs: reward self-reports for matching probe readings of the model's states.

On the present account, the design requirements follow from the conditions.

**Co-production.** If the report loss can reshape the probed activations, the model can learn to produce the probe feature *together with* the report. Report and reading then covary perfectly, but the reading measures the report. This violates A2's requirement that *S* precede and not be constituted by *T*. A purely synchronic criterion does not exclude it.

Detaching gradients at the probe read-out does not prevent this. The report loss still updates weights upstream of the probed layer, which changes the probed activations. What is needed is to freeze all parameters up to and including the probed layer, so that only a read-out pathway downstream is trained. This also blocks the Goodhart failure in which training changes what the probe direction encodes.

**Fork depth.** Suppose the report pathway reads the very direction the probe reads. Then the most downstream common source is the probed activation itself, and the anchored term expresses *exactly what the probe measures*, no more. To anchor to something deeper, the gates should depend on several diverse channels, such as:

- probes on different directions or layers,
- behavioural signatures like avoidance of a task, and
- downstream effects on performance.

The report pathway should then be checked by interpretability methods to see whether it branches from upstream of them.

**The held-out-channel test.** Anchor with some channels and withhold one functional signature of the target state from training. Then ask whether reports predict the withheld signature. Success is evidence that the term expresses the common source and not the trained channels. Failure is a defeater. This test is the AI counterpart of what the headache example was meant to illustrate.

## 6. How far anchored reports reach

The strongest objection to my earlier formulation was this. A probe-anchored "distress" concerns whatever the probe measures, and that state is measurable by construction. So anchoring does not reach the unmeasurable state, distress, that motivated the inquiry. The point that a model trained to say "zorp" would supply the same evidence seems to show that public content is idle. I accept much of this.

**Fit is not delivered.** Anchoring makes a self-report express *S*. It is testimony that the system is distressed only if *S* is distress. The unanchored system and the anchored system are on a par in this respect. The "zorp" point is correct about the *expressive* dimension: an anchored "zorp" would express *S* just as well. It is not correct about the semantic dimension. If *S* is distress, "distress" says something true and "zorp" says nothing in English.

The anchor does change something relevant to fit. If the gated channels are chosen as functional signatures of distress, the fork rule makes *S* their common source. That makes *S* a functionalist candidate for distress. It does not show that *S* is felt.

**Measurement is relocated, not removed.** Validating channels against the functional roles of the target is calibration, and verifying A2 requires interpretability. What changes is what must be measured.

- An unanchored report becomes evidence about *S* only through *occasion-by-occasion* access to *S* (calibration) or through mechanistic inspection that discovers an *S*-to-*T* pathway nobody had reason to expect.
- An anchored report requires knowledge of the training setup, which secures A1, plus *structural* verification of the pathway. Neither requires access to *S* on the occasions about which the report informs.

**Reach is partial, and partly testable.** With diverse channels and a deep fork, the anchored term expresses a state that each channel indicates only partially. Reports can therefore inform about occurrences of *S* that no single trained channel registers, and the held-out-channel test checks this. Beyond every channel, the projection is inductive. I earlier charged brute-coincidence covariance with a projection problem, and this projection differs from that one: it rests on a known mechanism (A1 plus a verified fork) and on held-out successes. The inference has the same form as trusting a person's report of pain in a body part nobody is examining.

So the claim that anchored testimony "reaches where calibration cannot" survives only in a reduced form. It reaches past the *calibrated channels* to their common source. It does not reach past the source to the question of whether the source is distress.

## 7. Insufficiency, resolution, and the human evidence

Anchoring is not sufficient for token reliability. My earlier discussion risked a pattern in which every failure was assigned, after the fact, to an absent anchor or an untracked dimension. The safeguard against this is to specify resolution *independently* of the reliability data.

In the AI case this is straightforward. Resolution is read off the gate function. If reward depends on a thresholded probe reading, only presence is anchored and magnitude is not. In the human case, resolution is a developmental hypothesis about what caregivers' responses could depend on: presence, rough intensity, location, valence. It is not a claim to be fitted to whatever misreports turn up. The human evidence, read against these specifications, gives a mixed result.

**Process reports.** Nisbett and Bellows (1977) found that subjects' reports of what had influenced their judgments of a job applicant matched the predictions of observers who had not taken part, and did not match the actual influences. Gates for vocabulary like "I chose it because..." depend on whether an explanation is plausible to the hearer, not on the causal process behind the choice, so A1 fails *by the independent specification*. This is the human analogue of the base model. The speaker says what anyone holding the shared theory would say about someone in their position.

**Choice blindness.** I earlier assimilated this to reason-giving, which was wrong. The central result is that subjects fail to notice that the face handed back to them is not the one they chose. Their subsequent "I preferred this one" uses preference vocabulary that is plausibly anchored, since a child's reaching gates "want". The anchor fixes what the predicate expresses. It does not secure the *demonstrative identification* of the object, which depends on perception and memory. Even so, this is a case in which anchored vocabulary is misapplied in a way the view did not predict, and I count it as a clean illustration of insufficiency.

**Schwitzgebel and Haybron.** Some of Schwitzgebel's (2008) cases concern fine-grained structure, such as the extent of clear peripheral vision, which lies outside any plausible gate resolution. Others concern fairly coarse matters: whether an emotion is present and what it is like. Haybron (2008) documents systematic misreport of one's own standing affect. One partial explanation is that gates track episodes of expression, not standing moods, so the anchor for mood terms is weak. I offer that as a hypothesis, not a vindication. The coarse failures show that anchoring yields at most a defeasible default even within its resolution.

**Affect labelling.** Labelling an affect modulates it (Lieberman et al. 2007). A2 excludes only *constitution* of *S* by the report. It does not exclude later feedback, and the evidence suggests the labelled state precedes the label and is then damped. Feedback does degrade the report's evidential value for *S*'s later course, so the condition is graded in practice.

**Alexithymia.** On the interoceptive-deficit account (Brewer, Cook & Bird 2016), *S* is poorly represented. A2 fails, and terms get recruited to situational cues despite A1. Developmental and social-learning accounts would instead locate the failure in A1, through gates unlinked to the child's affect. Either way it is an anchor failure, but which condition fails is an empirical question the view leaves open.

## 8. Entitlement

I earlier modelled the hearer's entitlement on Burge's (2003) perceptual entitlement. That was the wrong analogue, since perceptual entitlement is a perceiver's entitlement to her own beliefs. The analogue for hearers is the Acceptance Principle (Burge 1993). It grounds a default entitlement to accept content presented as true by a rational source. Whether AI systems are rational sources in that sense is part of what is in question, so the principle cannot be invoked here.

The literature on instruments and testimony (Goldberg 2010; Freiman & Miller 2020; Green & Michel 2022) asks when machine outputs are assertions as opposed to readings. My three-way distinction in §2 is a version of that question, and the anchor condition is a proposal about where the line falls for self-report.

On the reductionism debate (Coady 1992; Fricker 1994; Lackey 2008), the position I hold has two levels.

- **At the level of the source**, entitlement for AI self-report must be *earned*. It rests on positive knowledge that A1 holds, that the fork has been verified, and that maintenance and resolution are as specified.
- **At the level of the token**, once that knowledge is in place, individual reports may be accepted without checking each one, unless a defeater is present.

The asymmetry with unanchored reports is real but conditional. For unanchored reports, no amount of source-level knowledge of the *training setup* yields token-level acceptance about the system's own states, because the setup gives no reason to expect any self-ascriptive pathway.

I concede that for current deployed systems defeaters are pervasive: persona effects, unknown resolution, unverified forks, and susceptibility to Goodhart effects. For those systems the default does not currently activate. In practice, then, the anchor view and "one input among several" do not now diverge for existing systems. They diverge in what they say would *make* a difference: a training regime satisfying A1–A3, with verification, as opposed to ever more calibration against states we cannot measure.

The entitlement is graded, because it is stronger as gate dependence is stronger, resolution finer, and verification more thorough. The categorical claim is only this: where A1 fails for self-ascription, as it does for pretraining by design, the setup confers no first-personal standing at all.

## 9. Etiology and the synchronic

The synchronic view is right that, at a time, the mechanism does the evidential work. Etiology adds three things.

**Target fixation.** Etiology settles which of the states the mechanism is sensitive to the report *expresses*. Covariance cannot do this, and the fork rule can, up to residual indeterminacy that shows up as resolution.

**Counterfactual scope.** Etiology settles which variations count as the relevant ones for counterfactual sensitivity: variation in the gated state, along the gated dimensions. The co-production case satisfies covariance and sensitivity perfectly and is excluded only by this structure.

**Access.** For the hearer, knowledge of the training setup is often the only route to knowing which pathway to expect. Interpretability confirms that pathway. It does not tell us what to look for.

**Swampman.** A molecular duplicate of an anchored speaker, a Swampman in Davidson's (1987) sense, has an *S*-to-*T* pathway but no history that selected it. On the view, his self-reports lack first-personal standing at creation. A hearer who knows the duplication can still use them as constructed indicators, with the target read off the original's fork. They acquire anchors as soon as gates start to depend on his states. This is a cost for those with the opposite intuition, a cost teleosemanticists generally accept (Millikan 1984). Its practical relevance is small, because AI systems are not duplicates of anchored speakers.

## 10. Conclusion

The bare fact that a self-report vocabulary was learned from others' reports does not defeat it. What makes self-reports expressions of the reporter's own states is an anchor, consisting of four elements:

1. Gates that depended on the learner's state through a channel independent of the report, holding fixed the learner's situation.
2. A recruited pathway whose source is the common upstream state of those channels and the report.
3. Maintenance of that pathway.
4. A resolution read off the gates.

The account has five main consequences:

- Base models' first-person reports are world-directed reports about represented speakers. That is the precise form of the gaming problem, and it is established from the training objective without measurement.
- Confidence calibration and self-prediction training can anchor self-ascriptive vocabulary. Ordinary training of report outputs against fixed preferences cannot.
- Probe-based anchoring needs frozen upstream layers, diverse channels, and held-out-channel tests. Without them, the anchored term expresses only what the probe measures.
- Anchored reports reach beyond their training channels to the channels' common source. They do not reach beyond that source to the question of whether it is distress.
- Hearers' entitlement must be earned at the level of the source. For current systems it has not yet been earned.

Reliability testing remains essential. Its role is to verify anchors, map their resolution, and test their reach. On this account it cannot be a substitute for asking whether the reports have an anchor at all.

major: 1. The situation-conditionality clause, which is the paper's only device for separating self-ascriptive from world-directed terms, does not work for the systems the paper is about. A1 requires that 'holding fixed what L was confronted with, variation in S made a difference to the gates.' For the child this can be read as actual variation: pain varies with sensitization, fatigue and individual differences given a fixed injury. For a deterministic forward pass, however, there is no internal-state variation at all once the input and weights are fixed. With sampling, the only variation is sampling noise. So the clause must be read interventionally: had S been different, holding the input fixed, the gate would have differed. On that reading every internal representation upstream of the channel passes, including representations of the situation. In the confidence-calibration case (§4.3), intervening on the model's representation that the question is hard, or that this topic is obscure, changes correctness while the question is held fixed. That representation is a representation of the situation. A1 therefore does not tell us whether 'I'm unsure' becomes self-ascriptive or a world-directed report about question difficulty. Lindsey's injections are exactly such interventions on situation-representations ('bread'), and A1 read interventionally does not exclude them either. The author is caught in a dilemma. The interventionist reading makes the self/world distinction vacuous. A statistical reading (actual variation across training episodes given the situation) reintroduces exactly the correlational considerations §3 claims to have eliminated, and for deterministic models it yields almost no qualifying variation. The verdicts in §4.3, §4.5 and §5 all depend on this clause, so the authors need either a principled reading that avoids both horns or a different criterion. In §4.4 a base model's 'I am in pain' expresses the *content* of a representation (that the speaker of the text is in pain), with the model's state as mere vehicle. In anchored cases, a term expresses a state of L 'as L's condition.' What happens when the anchored state is itself a representation? This is the default for post-trained models. Suppose gates depend on behavioural channels (task avoidance, refusals, degraded performance) and those behaviours are driven by the model's representation of the Assistant persona's condition. Recent interpretability work on persona directions is relevant here (e.g. Chen et al. 2025 on 'persona vectors'). Then the paper's own content rule makes the most downstream common source of channels and report a persona representation, and A1 is satisfied. Is the anchored 'distress' then self-ascriptive, expressing a state of the model, or world-directed, expressing the represented distress of a character? The paper gives no criterion. Without a restricted space of admissible 'state-types', the most downstream common source is just the total proximal computational state. In the child, 'most downstream' should select an expressive or premotor bottleneck (a vocal-distress readiness state) rather than the central pain state the author wants. Taking the most *downstream* source also sits poorly with the claim that channel diversity pushes content *upstream*. The author owes three things. The first is an account of admissible state-types. If these are 'features' identified by interpretability, then the target-fixing work is done synchronically, which weakens T1. The second is an argument that 'most downstream' tracks the intended depth. (c) Real preference data are judgments over whole transcripts, and raters penalize mismatches between a model's self-descriptions and its behaviour elsewhere in the same conversation. The paper should address whether anchoring is plausible for attitudes at all, or only for sensations and affect. Finally, Bar-On's neo-expressivism is not a causal-historical theory of what an avowal expresses.
